To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the US is likely to experience a very rapid deterioration in its net foreign asset position, and that it is likely to be forced to cut its consumption of foreign goods and services by at least 8 per cent of GDP by the end of this decade.
the US's net external debt is likely to increase from 25 per cent to 35 per cent of GDP over the next decade.

the United States' current account balance will probably deteriorate further and that, if it does, the US will become an even larger net debtor to foreigners and the US's net income from abroad, which is already negative, will turn even more negative.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: 1) How large can the US trade deficit get before the dollar depreciates sharply and the economy slows down, and what will be the effect on the current account as the US net foreign asset position deteriorates?
the possibility that the US may not be able to sustain a trade deficit of the magnitude that has been forecast.

a simple question: can a country with a current account deficit of the magnitude of that of the United States, and with a foreign asset position of the magnitude of the US's net debt position, continue indefinitely to finance this deficit with a combination of foreign borrowing and the accumulation of foreign liabilities in the form of direct investment and other assets?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the US's net creditor position will continue to decline in the near future, but that this will be a gradual process.

the US's net debtor position has been increasing at a rate which, in a world where the US's creditworthiness is not questioned, can be sustained indefinitely, but that if there is a loss of confidence in the US's capacity to repay, the position is unsustainable.
the US is on the verge of becoming a debtor nation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the US is now in the midst of a major structural change.
the US has been able to finance its current account deficit by attracting large capital inflows from the rest of the world, but that the ability of the US to do so is now in question.

the US is now in a position where it has to choose between two options: either it can accept a substantial deterioration in its balance of payments position, with a consequent increase in the burden of debt servicing and the risk that it may have to default; or else it can accept a large reduction in its standard of living and a substantial increase in its rate of unemployment....
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a world of floating exchange rates, the current account balance of the United States cannot be expected to improve in the absence of a significant rise in the dollar.
the US economy has become more and more dependent on a flow of funds from the rest of the world to keep it going.
the US economy has become more vulnerable to external shocks than it was a decade ago.
